phrases.text: Coding agents rebuild the same integrations again and again:
payment gating, paying clients, the same glue code.
Every rebuild burns tokens, and it can still fail its tests.
Our first user is a developer whose agent must add x402 payments
to a TypeScript MCP server, like this one.
A few files, easy to get wrong, and someone has already built them.
Code search gives you code, but not whether it fits your repository.
Coverage products pay out after something breaks.
Nobody answers before you pay:
does this fit, is it safe, and is it cheaper than building?
Price a release by what it saves.
A benchmark measures the saving, and the price can be at most thirty percent of it,
so the buyer always comes out ahead.
No evidence, no sale.
Before writing code, the agent asks Lemma through our local bridge.
This request is all the bridge sends about your project:
the task, the language, the Node version, the package manager, the module system and one dependency version.
No source code, no file paths.
If nothing fits, the answer is free.
A capability we don't have yet, or a JavaScript project we don't support:
build it yourself, nothing is charged.
Matching is deterministic, so no model decides a match or a price.

segments.question: Why on chain, why Arbitrum, why Stylus?
segments.speaker: Awaan

phrases.text: A refund promise means little if the seller holds the money,
so a registry contract on Arbitrum holds the provider's bond.
The agent pays in USDC and never needs ETH.
And we wrote the score once in Rust:
the same code runs as a Stylus contract and in our server, so they always agree.
Here is a real purchase from October first, on Arbitrum Sepolia.
The agent paid zero point two five USDC over x402.
The buyer signed, and our facilitator sent the transaction and paid the gas.
Next, the provider's bond is reserved for this purchase, and the warranty becomes active.
The agent applied the patch and its tests passed,
and the result was recorded on chain, into the Stylus score engine.
Now the case that matters: a second purchase, where the project's tests failed.
The failure was recorded on chain,
and the bond paid zero point two five USDC back to the buyer's refund address.
And it still holds today.
This read-only check runs against the chain:
the contract code matches, the wiring is right, the registry is solvent,
and the score is recomputed from both outcomes.
Every check passed.
We tested the hard paths.
A lost answer is recovered without paying twice.
Spending limits refuse before anything is signed.
Changed payment terms are never paid.
And the contracts have fuzz and invariant tests.
We cut on purpose: no marketplace, no mainnet, no fee split yet.
First we proved the whole loop: pay, apply, test, refund.
And the trade-offs, out loud.
A team key judges failures for now.
Matching reads only metadata, so it covers fewer projects but never sees your code.
And one owner key holds the contracts until a multisig.
Not covered yet: independent evaluators, mainnet custody,
reorg detection in our indexer, and sandboxed tests on macOS.
Next: measured benchmarks for every release, outside providers, independent evaluators, an audit, then Arbitrum One.
Lemma: agents stop paying to rediscover solved work.
